world.era: ancient India, the time of the Buddha
world.setting: The banyan groves and river country of northern India: a brahmin's village, the ascetics in the forest, a merchant city, and one ferry crossing returned to twice.

siddhartha.name: Siddhartha
siddhartha.look: a young Indian brahmin man with a shaved head and a plain ochre robe, lean from fasting, ancient India

govinda.name: Govinda
govinda.look: a devoted young Indian monk in a saffron robe, softer-featured, always half a step behind, ancient India

vasudeva.name: Vasudeva
vasudeva.look: an old Indian ferryman with a white beard and a weathered wrap, standing at a pole on a wooden raft, ancient India

kamala.name: Kamala
kamala.look: an elegant Indian courtesan in red and gold silk with heavy earrings, composed, ancient India

kamaswami.name: Kamaswami
kamaswami.look: a heavyset middle-aged Indian merchant in embroidered cloth, rings on his fingers, ancient India

shore.look: the great river at the ferry crossing, flat brown water, a wooden raft drawn up on the bank

objects.why: the river IS the book's argument — it is everywhere at once, and it is the teacher
the banyan and the mango grove: where teaching happens, and where he sleeps
leaving is the recurring act — he walks away from every answer he is given
the father he leaves, and the son who leaves him the same way
the night watches: the ferryman and the sleepless

spine.claim: Everything a good teaching can give him, he already has, and it is not enough.
He refuses the perfect teacher, because a teaching cannot transmit the one thing he wants.
He goes all the way into appetite, and it hollows him out exactly as promised.
The ferryman teaches nothing; the river does, by refusing to be a sequence.
He is made to suffer his own leaving from the other side, and that is the last lesson.
